Let $X$ and $Y$ be continuous random variables with the joint probability density function 

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2}, & (x,y)\in D, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

If $F(x,y)$ is the joint CDF of $X$ and $Y,$ find $F(0,\frac{1}{2}).$
question.worked_solution:
If $X$ and $Y$ are continuous random variables with the joint probability density function $f(x,y),$ then the corresponding joint CDF is given by

$$
F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)={\int }_{-\infty }^{y}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}f(u,v)\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v.
$$

Let's draw the point $(0,\frac{1}{2})$ on our diagram. Let's also consider the region $Δ$ that lies below and to the left of this point.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14211556/assets/a5f876c9351040845fcc5e6839f4ca776fe22988a5e4c814d4a7b063692f083c.png)

Using the definition of the joint CDF, we have

$$
F(0,\frac{1}{2})=P(X<0,Y<\frac{1}{2})={\int }_{-\infty }^{1/2}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}f(u,v)\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v.
$$

For the purposes of computation, we're only interested in the region inside $Δ$ where $f(x,y)$ is nonzero. This is given by

$$
D\cap Δ=\{(x,y)\,:\,-1\le x\le 0,\,0\le y\le \frac{1}{2}\}.
$$

 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{1/2}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}f(u,v)\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}{\int }_{-1}^{0}(\frac{9}{2}{u}^{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}{[\frac{3}{2}{u}^{3}{v}^{2}]}_{u=-1}^{u=0}\,\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}(0+\frac{3}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}v \\  & ={[\frac{{v}^{3}}{2}]}_{v=0}^{v=1/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{16}-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$
